body:
Thermal electricity generation

In a conventional thermal power station, energy released from burning a fuel is converted into electricity. In a typical coal-fired station, coal combustion produces heat, which generates high-pressure steam. The steam drives a turbine connected to an electrical generator.

A gas-based power station uses natural gas as fuel. In a gas turbine, hot gases drive the turbine directly. In a combined-cycle plant, useful heat from the gas turbine's exhaust can also produce steam to generate additional electricity. Both are thermal technologies, but their fuels and methods differ.

Lignite is a relatively low-rank form of coal, commonly called brown coal. Gujarat has lignite resources and power stations that use this fuel. Coal-fired, lignite-fired and natural-gas-fired stations are all examples of fossil-fuel-based electricity generation.

Important thermal power stations in Gujarat

The following associations are useful for geographical identification. The stations are identified in Gujarat State Electricity Corporation Limited's power-station disclosures, with the station list and capacities reported as on 1 May 2024. The locations and fuel categories are the focus here; historical station capacities should not be mistaken for a later live capacity statement.

Power stationLocationFuel category
WanakboriKheda districtCoal
Ukai ThermalTapi districtCoal
SikkaJamnagar districtCoal
GandhinagarGandhinagar districtCoal
Kutch LigniteKachchh districtLignite
Bhavnagar LigniteBhavnagar districtLignite
UtranSurat districtNatural gas
DhuvaranAnand districtNatural gas

Ukai is especially important for avoiding confusion. The name is associated with both a coal-based thermal power station and a hydroelectric power station. A place name alone does not determine a plant's energy source.

What determines the usefulness of thermal power?

Thermal power stations are important because their output can generally be scheduled according to the availability of fuel and the operating capability of the plant. They can support electricity demand when sunlight or wind is insufficient. However, coal and gas supplies may be affected by mining, transport, import prices, fuel availability and operating restrictions.

Burning fossil fuels releases carbon dioxide. Coal combustion also creates other pollution-control challenges. Natural gas generally produces less carbon dioxide per unit of heat released than coal when burnt, but it is still a fossil fuel. Methane leakage along the gas supply chain is an additional environmental concern.

Nuclear electricity at Kakrapar

Nuclear power converts energy released by nuclear fission into heat, which is then used to generate electricity. Unlike coal or natural gas, the source of heat is a nuclear reaction rather than combustion.

Gujarat's principal nuclear generating location is Kakrapar, near Surat. The Nuclear Power Corporation of India Limited identifies 4 operating units at Kakrapar in its 2026 operating records:

  • Units 1 and 2: 220 MW each.
  • Units 3 and 4: 700 MW each.

The combined installed capacity of these 4 units is 1,840 MW. Units 3 and 4 began commercial operation on 30 June 2023 and 31 March 2024, respectively. These are generating-unit capacities and dates, not figures for Gujarat's entire nuclear electricity allocation or consumption.

Nuclear electricity is non-fossil but non-renewable. It does not require burning coal or natural gas during generation, but conventional nuclear reactors use finite mineral fuel. Nuclear power should not be included under solar or wind capacity simply because it is a non-fossil source.

Why conventional generation remains relevant

Gujarat's industrial demand requires reliable electricity across different hours and seasons. Dispatchable thermal and nuclear generation can contribute to this requirement alongside renewable power, hydropower, electricity imports and other flexibility arrangements. The amount each source actually generates depends on plant availability, fuel, system demand and operating conditions.

Prelims focus

  • Wanakbori, Ukai Thermal, Sikka and Gandhinagar are associated with coal-fired generation.
  • Kutch Lignite and Bhavnagar Lignite are associated with lignite-based generation.
  • Utran is associated with gas-based power generation.
  • Kakrapar is a nuclear power station near Surat.
  • Kakrapar's 4 operating units have a combined capacity of 1,840 MW in NPCIL's 2026 records.
  • Trap: Ukai Thermal and Ukai Hydro are not the same generating station.

[References: NCERT, Class 8 Geography, Resources and Development, Chapter 3, 'Mineral and Power Resources,' printed pp. 31–35; Gujarat State Electricity Corporation Limited, 'Proactive Disclosures under RTI,' thermal and hydro station tables dated 1 May 2024; Nuclear Power Corporation of India Limited, 'Operating Performance,' Kakrapar units and commercial-operation dates, FY 2026–27 records consulted 16 November 2026.]

title: Conventional Electricity: Coal, Lignite, Gas and Nuclear Power

body:
Why Gujarat is suitable for renewable energy

Gujarat contains large areas with substantial sunlight, coastal and inland locations with useful wind resources, and river systems capable of supporting hydropower. These natural conditions have encouraged the development of different renewable electricity technologies.

Renewable energy sources are widely available in nature, but electricity generation from them depends on local conditions. A solar plant needs adequate solar radiation; a wind turbine needs suitable wind; and a hydroelectric station needs an appropriate flow of water and sufficient difference in water level.

Solar energy

Solar photovoltaic (PV) cells convert sunlight directly into electrical energy. Several cells are assembled into modules or panels, and many panels can be connected to form a solar power plant. Solar thermal applications are different: they use the Sun's heat, for example in solar water heaters or solar cookers.

Gujarat's sunny western and northern regions provide favourable conditions for solar power development. Two important geographical examples are:

  • Charanka Solar Park: Located at Charanka village in Santalpur taluka of Patan district. It is a recognised solar park development in north Gujarat.
  • Khavda renewable energy developments: Located in the Kachchh region, where large-scale solar and wind projects are being developed in phases. The announced capacity of a park is not necessarily the capacity already commissioned.

Solar power can also be produced on rooftops and in smaller installations closer to consumers. Large solar parks and rooftop solar systems use the same basic photovoltaic principle, although their locations, connections and purposes may differ.

Wind energy

Wind turbines convert the kinetic energy of moving air into rotational motion that drives a generator. Wind power is particularly relevant in suitable parts of Kachchh and Saurashtra, where coastal and other favourable wind conditions support generation.

Wind generation changes with wind speed and operating conditions. An installed wind turbine therefore does not produce its rated output continuously. A site with stronger or more consistent winds can generate more electricity than another site with similar installed capacity.

Hydroelectric power

Hydroelectricity is generated when flowing or falling water drives turbines connected to electrical generators. In a storage-based hydroelectric project, water held behind a dam can be released through the generating system when suitable operating conditions permit.

Gujarat examples include Ukai Hydro on the Tapi River and Kadana Hydro on the Mahi River. The Sardar Sarovar project on the Narmada is another major hydroelectric association.

Large hydropower and small hydropower both use flowing water. In India, small hydropower projects have installed capacities up to 25 MW and large hydropower projects exceed 25 MW, but both are counted within renewable energy in the Ministry of New and Renewable Energy's renewable-capacity statistics.

Different technologies, different conditions

Solar PV generation generally follows available sunlight and is absent at night unless another source or stored electricity supplies the load. Wind power can be available during the day or night but depends on wind conditions. Hydropower can offer greater control over the timing of generation where water storage and operating conditions permit, although output still depends on water availability.

A wind-solar hybrid project combines wind and solar generation in an arrangement intended to make use of both resources. It does not guarantee constant electricity supply; periods of low wind and low sunlight can still occur together.

Renewable resource potential and installed capacity

Resource potential describes the energy that might be developed under specified assumptions. Installed capacity describes the rated generating equipment that has actually been installed. Electricity generation is the energy produced during a defined period.

For a large project such as Khavda, proposed, under-construction and commissioned capacities must be distinguished. A statement that a development is planned for a particular capacity does not establish that all of it is producing electricity.

Prelims focus

  • Charanka Solar Park is in Patan district.
  • Khavda renewable energy developments are in Kachchh.
  • Kachchh and Saurashtra are important regions for wind-energy development.
  • Ukai Hydro is associated with the Tapi River; Kadana Hydro with the Mahi River.
  • Solar PV directly converts sunlight into electricity; solar thermal systems use solar heat.
  • Trap: A renewable project's planned capacity is not necessarily its commissioned capacity.

[References: NCERT, Class 8 Geography, Resources and Development, Chapter 3, 'Mineral and Power Resources,' printed pp. 32–36; NCERT, Class 12 Geography, India: People and Economy, Chapter 7, 'Mineral and Energy Resources,' printed pp. 82–83; SJVN Limited, 'Charanka Solar Power Station,' project location and commissioning details, consulted 16 November 2026; Press Information Bureau, Ministry of Power, release on Khavda solar development dated 15 March 2024; Gujarat State Electricity Corporation Limited, hydro station disclosures dated 1 May 2024.]

body:
Why electricity statistics need careful interpretation

Electricity-sector statements often use the words capacity, generation, demand and consumption. These measure related but different things. Understanding the distinction is essential before comparing coal, solar, wind or other sources.

  • Installed capacity: The rated ability of generating equipment to produce electricity, usually expressed in MW or GW.
  • Electricity generation: The quantity of electrical energy actually produced during a period, usually expressed in MWh, MU or BU.
  • Electricity demand: The rate at which users require power at a particular time, often expressed in MW.
  • Electricity consumption: The quantity of electricity used by consumers over a period, commonly reported in units or MU.

Units used in energy reports

UnitMeaningMeasures
MWMegawattPower or generating capacity
GW1,000 MWLarge-scale power capacity
kWhKilowatt-hourElectrical energy
MU1 million kWhElectricity generated or consumed
BU1 billion kWhLarge quantities of electricity generated or consumed

For example, a 1 MW generator operating at a constant output of 1 MW for 1 hour produces 1 MWh, equivalent to 1,000 kWh. If it produces less than its rated output or is not operating for the entire hour, its energy generation will be lower.

Gujarat's renewable capacity at the end of 2025–26

The Ministry of New and Renewable Energy's Renewable Energy Statistics 2025–26 provides a dated snapshot of the state's electricity sector. The following figures refer to installed capacity as on 31 March 2026; they are not live figures for November 2026.

  • Total renewable installed capacity: Approximately 47.18 GW.
  • Total non-renewable installed capacity: Approximately 24.51 GW.
  • Solar installed capacity: Approximately 29.30 GW.
  • Wind installed capacity: Approximately 15.64 GW.
  • Renewable share of total installed capacity: 65.81%.

These statistics show that renewable sources represented the larger share of Gujarat's installed generating capacity at the end of the reporting year. Solar contributed more installed capacity than wind.

Gujarat's renewable electricity generation during 2025–26

During the financial year 2025–26, Gujarat generated approximately 67.83 BU of electricity from renewable sources. This represented 46.31% of the state's total electricity generation reported for that year.

Within Gujarat's renewable electricity generation during 2025–26, wind contributed 49.69%, while solar contributed 40.36%. This is an important contrast: solar had more installed capacity than wind, but wind produced more renewable electricity during that reporting year.

Why the 2 percentages are different

Installed capacity indicates how much power equipment is rated to produce under specified conditions. Actual generation depends on operating hours, weather, fuel availability, maintenance and system requirements. A solar plant cannot generate from sunlight at night, and a wind turbine cannot generate its rated output when the wind is insufficient.

Consequently, 65.81% renewable installed capacity does not mean that 65.81% of electricity was generated from renewable sources. The capacity percentage describes installed equipment on 31 March 2026. The generation percentage describes electricity produced over the entire 2025–26 financial year.

These percentages also have different denominators: total installed capacity for the first measure and total electricity generation for the second. They cannot be used interchangeably.

Statistical qualification: Renewable-capacity totals can change after the reporting date. Different official tables may also use different accounting methods, such as location-based generating capacity or allocated shares of generating stations. Always compare the date, coverage and definition before concluding that 2 figures conflict.

What the figures reveal about energy transition

The 2025–26 snapshot shows the expansion of Gujarat's renewable generating equipment. It does not imply that fossil-fuel-based generation has disappeared or that renewable energy can satisfy demand at every hour without support from the broader electricity system.

Industrial demand continues during evening and night hours. Therefore, growth in renewable capacity must be understood together with the availability of other generating sources, transmission facilities, storage and measures to match electricity demand with supply.

Prelims focus

  • 1 GW equals 1,000 MW.
  • 1 MU equals 1 million kWh; 1 BU equals 1 billion kWh.
  • Gujarat's renewable installed capacity was approximately 47.18 GW on 31 March 2026.
  • Solar capacity was approximately 29.30 GW and wind capacity approximately 15.64 GW on that date.
  • Renewable electricity generation was approximately 67.83 BU during 2025–26, representing 46.31% of total generation.
  • Trap: The percentage share of installed capacity is not the same as the percentage share of electricity generation.

[References: Ministry of New and Renewable Energy, Government of India, Renewable Energy Statistics 2025–26, Chapter 11, 'Gujarat,' printed pp. 54–60, particularly Table 11.1.1, the solar and wind capacity discussion, and section 11.3, consulted 16 November 2026; NCERT, Class 11 Economics, Indian Economic Development, Chapter 8, 'Infrastructure,' section 8.5, printed pp. 144–149.]
